newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel Kabila returns after refugee crisis.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel Kabila returns after refugee crisis.

text.p: Zairean rebel chief Laurent Kabila returned to Lubumbashi on Monday after tackling a refugee crisis in the north-east and holding talks with a Japanese envoy.

Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, moved back to the mineral-rich province as his forces closed in on the town of Kikwit, bringing the war closer to the capital Kinshasa.
"We are consolidating our advance on Kikwit and the town is now vulnerable," Kabila told Reuters on arrival in Lubumbashi, the country's second largest city,.
He added: "But we are still open to a peaceful transfer of power in Kinshasa. We are still committed to meeting the other side to talk."

Earlier during a stop-over in the north-eastern provincial capital Kisangani where he had gone to personally intervene in a crisis over Rwandan Hutu refugees, Kabila met a Japanese envoy and said force was still an option if a peaceful transition of power in Kinshasa proved impossible.
In his first contact with the Japanese government, Kabila received a delegation led by Ryuichi Shoji, director of the African division at the ministry of foreign affairs in Tokyo.
Kabila told Shoji he had been asking for negotiations with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko for the past six months.

"I'm still asking for negotiations because I believe a peaceful transfer of power in Kinshasa is the best thing. But if we do not get a positive response on peace talks, we leave the military option open," he said.

The Japanese team, visiting Kabila at his headquarters in the eastern Zairean border city of Goma, raised concerns over a transitional government in Kinshasa, democracy, good governance, human rights and the issue of Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire.
Delegation members said they were on a fact-finding mission to learn about the economic and political objectives of the rebel Alliance, which has seized more than half of Zaire.
They said they wanted to learn how Kabila planned to reform the economy and about his attitude to private investment and the economic role of any future Zairean government formed under him.

Kabila, who will meet U.S. envoy Bill Richardson on Wednesday, said in Goma on Monday the rebels were gaining ground against Mobutu but at the same time co-operating with U.S. and South African mediation efforts.
"We are committed to dialogue but that doesn't stop us from making military gains," Kabila told Reuters on arrival in Goma from Kisangani for talks with commanders of the rebel alliance.

He said rebels had reached the area around Bondo, a town 300 km (185 miles) east of Gbadolite, Mobutu's northern jungle palace, and were consolidating their approach to the town of Kikwit 390 km (240 miles) east of the Zairean capital Kinshasa.

Richardson said on arrival in Kinshasa on Monday: "The United States believes that there can be no military solution to the crisis, but rather a negotiated settlement leading to an inclusive transitional government and fair and free elections."
Kabila said final touches were being put to a pact mediated by South Africa and both sides had almost agreed on a venue for face-to-face talks but some details had still to be worked out.
The rebel chief says he will only meet Mobutu to discuss how he will stand down as Zaire's leader after 32 years in power.
Kabila said he was committed to an independent inquiry by the United Nations into reports of killings of Rwandan refugees.
Up to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees disappeared from their camps in rebel-held east Zaire last week and fled to the jungle.
But Kabila said he wanted rebel officials to sit in on the inquiry as observers and wanted it to include members of the Organisation of African Unity and neighbouring countries.
